problem: End-to-end visual navigation models (GNM/ViNT/NoMaD) have no explicit geometric constraints, so obstacle avoidance is unreliable on new platforms and with unfamiliar obstacles. Classical geometric planners are safe but cannot handle image goals.
motivation: Real-robot deployment needs both goal-image semantic reasoning and reliable collision avoidance. Prior hybrids (e.g. Less Is More) inject geometry only into training, so inference still relies on the VFM's implicit avoidance. The paper adds an explicit geometric stage after VFM inference.
key_idea: Use a ViNT/NoMaD-style diffusion policy to produce semantic waypoint candidates, then refine them with a depth-based geometric planner (TTC safety filter, gradient-based trajectory optimization, temporal smoothing).
insight: Explicit post-hoc geometric refinement on depth improves obstacle avoidance without hurting goal-reaching. In the multi-obstacle ablation, the full planner reaches 80% SR versus 60% for Gradient-Only, 60% for TTC-Only and 40% for an APF replacement. TTC-Only oscillates left and right and is slow (33.86 s), so the combination and smoothing matter. NoMaD fails badly with obstacles (0% SR multi-obstacle), which the authors attribute to executing the first diffusion sample without geometric refinement.
method: Semantic Reasoning Module: EfficientNet-B0 encodes the observation sequence and goal image; a Transformer produces context c_t; a diffusion head outputs short-horizon waypoints (NoMaD-like, goal mask removed); trained with denoising loss plus auxiliary temporal-distance loss.
Depth back-projection: depth is converted into 2D ground-plane obstacle points (x=z, y=-(u-cx)z/fx), subsampled, and indexed with a KD-tree for fast distance queries.

TTC risk estimation: uses the first-decile center depth across frames to estimate approach speed and TTC. If TTC < tau_ttc or depth < d_safe, emergency mode suppresses high-risk motion components and lateral motion when side space is small.

Gradient-based optimizer: refines each candidate trajectory by minimizing a cost of collision (cubic hinge, d_s=0.25 m), smoothness, deviation from the original trajectory, minus progress and clearance rewards; the argmin-cost trajectory is chosen.
Temporal smoothing: exponential filter w_hat_t = beta*w_hat_{t-1} + (1-beta)*w_t, plus command-increment limits to suppress jitter in narrow passages.
Go2 dataset fine-tuning: a dedicated Unitree Go2 dataset is collected for platform-specific training (scale not given).

setting.backbone: EfficientNet-B0 + Transformer + diffusion policy head (ViNT/NoMaD-style), trained/fine-tuned; geometric planner is non-learned
setting.training_data: Self-collected Unitree Go2 navigation dataset (size unspecified); may start from ViNT/NoMaD-style pretraining (not stated)
setting.action_space: predicted waypoints converted to linear/angular velocity (v, omega); max 0.4 m/s, 0.8 rad/s

numbers_note: All results are small-sample real-robot trials (20/10/10 runs) on a custom Go2 setup; there are no standard benchmarks. Only the main method is listed; ablation variants (Gradient-Only 60%, TTC-Only 60%, APF-Only 40%) appear in Table 4.
results: On a Unitree Go2, SemGeoNav reaches 100% SR (obstacle-free, 29.29 s), 100% (single obstacle, 28.96 s) and 80% (multiple obstacles, 29.35 s). The strongest baseline, ViNT fine-tuned on Go2 data (ViNT-Go2), gets 100%, 90% and 50%; pretrained ViNT gets 85%, 90% and 40%; NoMaD gets 75%, 50% and 0%. SemGeoNav also has the shortest average times.
limitations: Very small evaluation: 10-20 trials per scenario, static obstacles only, a single robot and indoor scenes, with no statistical analysis.
Depth scale is not aligned with the model-predicted waypoint scale (stated as future work), and the TTC/safety thresholds are hand-tuned.

No comparison with other hybrid or geometry-supervised methods (e.g. Less Is More); the dataset is not described in detail, and ViNT-Go2 uses fine-tuning that may not match the SemGeoNav training data.
